subject: Archaeology
title: Sieving and Flotation: Finding the Tiny Stuff
description: Learn Sieving and Flotation: Finding the Tiny Stuff in one minute.

hook.text: The most important finds on a dig often fit on a fingertip — seeds, fish bones, and insect wings tell huge stories.

buildup.text: Soil from excavations is pushed through mesh sieves. Anything larger than the mesh holes is collected and sorted.

discovery.text: Flotation works differently: soil is stirred in water. Light organic material — seeds, charcoal — floats to the surface.

twist.text: A single charred seed can reveal what ancient people ate, what crops they grew, and what climate they lived in.

climax.text: Flotation at Çatalhöyük revealed the earliest known domesticated wheat — evidence that farming began in Turkey.

punchline.text: A seed smaller than a pea proved where farming began.

quiz.question: How does flotation help archaeologists?
options: It dissolves soil to expose buried structures
Light organic material like seeds and charcoal floats to the surface for collection
It measures the water content of soil to determine the age of deposits
